🖼️ Framing Our Work

Another way to cultivate literacy routines in our classrooms is to support students in learning to enter conversations with texts.

By teaching students to use the They Say / I Say framework, we can help them recognize that reading and writing are deeply social acts—opportunities to listen to the ideas of others and to craft thoughtful responses of their own. This routine demystifies academic writing, giving students practical tools to engage with arguments, respond to diverse perspectives, and develop their voices as writers.

Equally important, expanding our understanding of “text” to include visuals and multimodal artifacts makes this work accessible, concrete, and relevant to students’ daily lives. In turn, They Say / I Say routines contribute to a classroom community where students learn to navigate, question, and add to the conversations that shape the world around them.

📝What to Expect

In this module, you will

✅Explore the They Say / I Say framework as a way for students to enter conversations with texts.

✅Consider how “text” includes not just written words, but also visuals, multimodal artifacts, and everyday media.

✅Review a Writer’s Notebook routine using They Say / I Say with visual texts, followed by partner discussion.

✅Practice annotation with a written text in Google Docs to make “They Say / I Say” conversations visible.

✅ Join the They Say / I Say discussion to reflect on your experience and connect with other teachers.

✅Earn the They Say / I Say microcredential by reflecting with your facilitator on how you will adapt these strategies for your own students.

🧭 Explore and Learn

They Say / I Say

In They Say / I Say: The Moves that Matter in Academic Writing, Graff and Birkenstein describe academic writing as a “conversation” where students frame their arguments as a response to what others have said (They say) and use templates to help construct their own response (I say).

They explain:

One central goal of this book is to demystify academic writing by returning it to its social and conversational roots. Although writing may require some degree of quiet and solitude, the ‘they say / I say’ model shows students that they can best develop their arguments not just by looking inward but by doing what they often do in a good conversation with friends and family—by listening carefully to what others are saying and engaging with other views.

In other words, students learn to enter a conversation by first establishing “what others are saying” before introducing their own perspective as a response.

What is a Text?

In Academic Moves for College & Career Readiness, Burke and Gilmore define “text” as “a piece of writing, speech, video, or other artifact in its original format.” They emphasize that text “is not limited to printed words; it may include visuals, digital information, or material presented in a variety of other manners.”

To further this idea, Wilhelm, Bear, and Fachler (2020) highlight the importance of visual texts in literacy instruction:

Take a moment to consider the types of texts you encounter in your everyday life as you read the news, search for teaching tools, scan social media, and otherwise go about your day. What are the different text types you encounter in your job and social life? News articles are usually accompanied by images and/or videos; online resources for teaching include images, graphical representations of information, maps, charts and checklists; your social media newsfeeds likely contain a mixture of written texts with political cartoons, graphs, videos, and images. Reading visual texts, on their own and in conjunction with other texts, is a necessary part of literacy.

Cognitive research shows that learning often proceeds from the concrete to the abstract, and from the visual to the nonvisual. Universal Design for Learning (UDL) provides a framework for designing instruction that meets the needs of diverse learners, while visualization strategies can engage English learners and struggling readers through more immediate access points. And, of course, reading and creating meaning through visuals can be fun!

Together, these ideas invite us to think about what happens when we bring They Say / I Say into dialogue with a wide range of texts, including visuals. If academic writing is a conversation, then visual texts—political cartoons, infographics, advertisements, photographs—can also become part of that conversation. In the next section, we’ll explore how to use the They Say / I Say framework with visual texts to help students practice responding, analyzing, and adding their voices in ways that feel both concrete and accessible.

They Say / I Say with Visual Texts

One way to introduce the They Say / I Say framework with visual texts is through a quickwrite and partner discussion protocol. This routine builds on the Writer’s Notebook work from Module One by inviting students to respond quickly and often to different kinds of texts. Using a slideshow of visual texts—such as political cartoons, infographics, advertisements, or photographs—students can practice the They Say / I Say framework as a way to both notice arguments in visuals and develop their own responses.

Below is a student-facing slideshow that includes a range of visual texts, along with prompts for inviting students to analyze and discuss the visuals through the They Say / I Say framework. Note that the slideshow includes a number of visuals; the idea is for you to choose the visuals that best fit your students and teaching context, and/or to add other visuals you find for this purpose.

Process:

  1. Display each visual for 3-5 minutes. As the visual is displayed, students jot their responses to the visual in their Writer's Notebook:

  • They say… (What message or perspective does this visual communicate? What argument or claim is being made, directly or indirectly?)

  • I say… (How do I respond to this message? Do I agree, disagree, or want to complicate it? What evidence or reasoning supports my response?)

2. After analyzing a few visuals, have students turn to a partner and share their “They Say / I Say” responses. Encourage them to notice similarities, differences, and surprises in their responses.

3. Repeat the process with a number of visuals, so students have plenty of practice, and generate multiple short notebook entries during the routine.

Over time, this notebook practice creates a collection of quick, low-stakes responses to a variety of texts. These entries can serve as seeds for larger discussions, more developed written responses, or future argumentative writing.

Click here to make your own copy of the slideshow to adapt for your teaching context.

They Say / I Say through Annotation

Once students have practice with applying the They Say / I Say framework with visuals, a logical next step is for them to try out the framework in response to written texts. Annotation offers a way to make this conversation visible—literally writing in the margins to capture both what the text is saying and how the reader wants to respond. In this approach, students identify phrases or sentences in the text that they are interested in responding to. They highlight or underline the words or phrases (They Say) and then write their own responses as annotations (I Say). This early scaffolding through annotation helps students engage in a conversation with a single text.

After practicing this annotation approach, students are eventually ready to add in the skill of summarizing, paraphrasing, or quoting the “They Say” and writing more developed “I Say” responses.

Check out this slideshow with examples of students trying out They Say / I Say with annotation and in response to an article:

Next, take a look at the handout below to discover more about the templates from Graff and Berkenstein’s They Say / I Say.

These templates, also called sentence starters, stems, or frames, can help students make deliberate choices about responding to texts and using sources in their own writing.

They Say I Say Templates.pdf

Let's try it! Choose one article below and join the conversation.

Pick a topic that interests you and click on the article title to open it in a new window. Next, engage with the text using the “add comment” feature in Google Docs (click the comment symbol in the upper right-hand corner of the menu bar).

Highlight words, phrases, or sentences from the article that you find interesting (They Say), then add your response using the “I Say” concept. Consider trying out some of the They Say / I Say templates from the handout above.

  • Yes, Teens Are Glued to Their Screens, but Here is What We Are Missing (KQED)

  • Teens Say They Are Turning to AI For Friendship (AP News)

  • Phones and Other Tech Can Enhance Teens' Connection to Nature (The Conversation)

  • Study: Instagram influencers tend to promote more unhealthy foods than other celebrities (Science News for Students)

  • Kids wrote pleas to help unwanted shelter pups find homes; it worked (The Washington Post)

Be sure to comment on others’ responses to keep the conversation going. If you feel compelled, comment on more than one article!

💬 Try and Share

After trying out the annotation process, join the They Say / I say discussion and write a reflection about your experience with They Say / I Say.

  • What do you think about Graff and Birkenstein’s idea that engaging with a text is like entering a conversation?

  • What was it like for you to try out the They Say / I Say annotation process?

  • How might your students benefit from using the They Say / I Say templates? What might be challenging for them?

Your contributions help build a supportive environment where ideas can flourish, and together, we grow as educators.

When trying the They say/I say annotation process I was able to connect to the text in a personal way. I found the words and phrases that had an impact on me and thought about the meaning of the text. Students can benefit from using this process because it is low stakes, but high reward. When approaching the process as a conversation with the text the pressure is off students to write correct answers to the text. Instead they can "talk" to the text about their thoughts, feelings, and connections as if they are talking with a peer. They are then highly engaged with the text and deepen their understanding of the text without realizing it.

10:20 am

Engaging with the text is like entering a conversation. Getting involved with the text makes the main points and meaning clearer. It becomes participating instead of just listening/reading. The They Say/I Say annotation process helps clarify what the author is trying to convey. My students will benefit because it will force them to seek meaning and understanding of terms and ideas. The challenging part will be to put everything down that they are really questioning or unsure of meaning. Sometimes students are scared to be "wrong" or not "know" things. Sharing with peers their lack of knowledge in an area may be daunting at first.
